content: A perfect gas is defined as a gas in which intermolecular forces are entirely neglected. This assumption, in addition to the assumptions of an ideal gas, allows for the derivation of the equation of state for a perfect gas using kinetic theory or statistical mechanics. By neglecting intermolecular forces, calculations become significantly simpler and more straightforward. This simplification enables the application of the Ideal Gas Law without restrictions and avoids complications that may arise from intermolecular forces such as Van der Waals forces. In addition to the definition of a perfect gas, there are two further simplifications that can be made. While some textbooks may omit or combine these into a general definition of a perfect gas, for clarity, they are defined separately as follows: Thermally Perfect Gas A thermally perfect gas is one that satisfies the following conditions: The gas is in thermodynamic equilibrium. The gas is not undergoing any chemical reactions. The internal energy, enthalpy, and specific heat of the gas are functions of temperature only. These relationships can be expressed as: Internal energy: ( e = e(T) ) Enthalpy: ( h = h(T) ) Change in internal energy: ( de = C_v dT ) Change in enthalpy: ( dh = C_p dT ) This approximation is particularly useful for modeling systems where temperature fluctuations are not large enough to cause significant deviations from the thermally perfect gas model. For example, in an axial compressor, the temperature variations are typically small, making this model sufficiently accurate. In this case, heat capacity is allowed to vary with temperature, but molecular dissociation is not permitted. Calorically Perfect Gas The most restrictive gas model is the calorically perfect gas, which incorporates all the assumptions of a thermally perfect gas and adds the following condition: The specific heats (( C_v ) and ( C_p )) are constant. This leads to the following relationships: Internal energy: ( e = C_v T ) Enthalpy: ( h = C_p T ) Although this is the most constrained model, it can still provide accurate results for many practical calculations. For instance, if one were to model a single compression stage of an axial compressor (as mentioned earlier) using both a variable-( C_p ) model and a constant-( C_p ) model, the deviation between the two would likely be small. In fact, the magnitude of this deviation might be so minor that other factors, such as compressor tip-clearance, boundary layer or frictional losses, and manufacturing imperfections, would have a more significant impact on the final result than whether ( C_p ) was held constant.
